title: GATE Mathematics Topic Test: Linear Algebra — Set 1
titleEn: GATE Mathematics Topic Test: Linear Algebra — Set 1
titleHi: गेट गणित टॉपिक टेस्ट: रैखिक बीजगणित — सेट 1

questions.questionTextEn: Let $U$ and $W$ be distinct $4$-dimensional subspaces of a $5$-dimensional vector space $V$ over $\mathbb{R}$. What is $\dim(U \cap W)$?
questions.explanationEn: Since $U$ and $W$ are distinct $4$-dimensional subspaces of $V$, $U + W$ properly contains $U$, so $\dim(U + W) = 5$. By the dimension formula, $\dim(U \cap W) = \dim(U) + \dim(W) - \dim(U + W) = 4 + 4 - 5 = 3$.

questions.questionTextEn: Let $T: \mathbb{R}^4 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ be a linear transformation and $S: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^4$ be a linear transformation. Which of the following statements is always TRUE?
questions.explanationEn: Since $S \circ T: \mathbb{R}^4 \to \mathbb{R}^4$ factors through $\mathbb{R}^3$, we have $\operatorname{rank}(S \circ T) \le \min(\operatorname{rank}(S), \operatorname{rank}(T)) \le 3 < 4$. Therefore $S \circ T$ can never have full rank $4$, so it is never invertible.

questions.questionTextEn: Let $V$ be an $n$-dimensional vector space and $T: V \to V$ be a linear operator such that $T^2 = T$. Which of the following is necessarily equal to $V$?
questions.explanationEn: For any $v \in V$, write $v = (v - Tv) + Tv$. Since $T(v - Tv) = Tv - T^2 v = 0$, we have $v - Tv \in \ker(T)$ and $Tv \in \operatorname{im}(T)$, so $V = \ker(T) + \operatorname{im}(T)$. If $u \in \ker(T) \cap \operatorname{im}(T)$, then $u = Tw$ and $0 = Tu = T^2 w = Tw = u$. Thus $V = \ker(T) \oplus \operatorname{im}(T)$.

questions.questionTextEn: Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ with dual space $V^*$, and let $W$ be a subspace of $V$ with annihilator $W^0 = \{f \in V^* : f(w) = 0 \text{ for all } w \in W\}$. If $\dim(V) = 7$ and $\dim(W) = 3$, then $\dim(W^0)$ is:
questions.explanationEn: For any subspace $W$ of a finite-dimensional vector space $V$, $\dim(W) + \dim(W^0) = \dim(V)$ (since $W^0 \cong (V/W)^*$). Hence $\dim(W^0) = 7 - 3 = 4$.

questions.questionTextEn: Let $Q \in M_3(\mathbb{R})$ be an orthogonal matrix with $\det(Q) = -1$. Which of the following must be an eigenvalue of $Q$?
questions.explanationEn: Since $Q$ is orthogonal, $Q^T Q = I$. Thus $\det(Q + I) = \det(Q + Q Q^T) = \det(Q) \det(I + Q^T) = -\det(I + Q)$, which implies $2\det(Q + I) = 0$, so $\det(Q + I) = 0$. Therefore $-1$ is necessarily an eigenvalue of $Q$.

questions.questionTextEn: Let $A \in M_n(\mathbb{R})$ be a real symmetric matrix. Which of the following statements are ALWAYS true?
optionsEn: Eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues of $A$ are orthogonal with respect to the standard inner product
There exists an orthogonal matrix $Q$ such that $Q^T A Q$ is diagonal
$\operatorname{rank}(A)$ equals the number of non-zero eigenvalues of $A$ counted with algebraic multiplicity
questions.explanationEn: By the Real Spectral Theorem, real symmetric matrices have orthogonal eigenspaces for distinct eigenvalues (A), are orthogonally diagonalizable (B), and since they are diagonalizable, $\operatorname{rank}(A)$ equals the number of non-zero eigenvalues with multiplicity (C). (D) is false (e.g., $-I$ has eigenvalue $-1$).

questions.questionTextEn: Let $A \in M_n(\mathbb{R})$ be a real symmetric positive definite matrix. Which of the following statements are ALWAYS true?
optionsEn: All diagonal entries of $A$ are strictly positive
All off-diagonal entries of $A$ are non-negative
questions.explanationEn: Evaluating $e_i^T A e_i = a_{ii} > 0$ gives (A). All eigenvalues $\lambda_i > 0$, so $A^{-1}$ is symmetric with eigenvalues $1/\lambda_i > 0$ (B), and $\det(A) = \prod \lambda_i > 0$ (C). (D) is false since $\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ is positive definite with negative off-diagonal entries.

questions.questionTextEn:
What is the rank of the $4 \times 4$ real matrix
$$A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 \\ 3 & 5 & 7 & 9 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}?$$
questions.explanationEn: Notice that $R_3 = R_1 + R_2$ and $R_4 = R_2 - R_1$. Thus the row space is spanned by $R_1 = (1,2,3,4)$ and $R_2 = (2,3,4,5)$, which are linearly independent. Hence $\operatorname{rank}(A) = 2$.

questions.questionTextEn:
For what real value of $\alpha$ does the linear system
$$x + y + z = 2, \quad 2x + 3y + 2z = 5, \quad x + 2y + z = \alpha$$
have infinitely many solutions?
questions.explanationEn: Subtracting the first equation from the second yields $x + 2y + z = 3$. Since the left-hand side of the third equation is identical to $x + 2y + z$, the system is consistent (and of rank $2 < 3$, hence having infinitely many solutions) if and only if $\alpha = 3$.

questions.questionTextEn: What is the signature (number of positive eigenvalues minus number of negative eigenvalues) of the real quadratic form $q(x, y, z) = x^2 + 4xy + y^2 - z^2$?
questions.explanationEn: The symmetric matrix of $q$ is $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$. Its eigenvalues are $1 + 2 = 3$, $1 - 2 = -1$, and $-1$. Thus there is $1$ positive eigenvalue and $2$ negative eigenvalues, giving signature $1 - 2 = -1$.

questions.questionTextEn: Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional inner product space and $T: V \to V$ be a linear operator. Which of the following subspace identities ALWAYS holds?
questions.explanationEn: A vector $v \in V$ lies in $\ker(T^*)$ iff $\langle T^* v, u \rangle = 0$ for all $u \in V$, iff $\langle v, Tu \rangle = 0$ for all $u \in V$, iff $v \in (\operatorname{im}(T))^\perp$. Options (B) and (C) fail for non-normal operators, and $\ker(T^* T) = \ker(T)$.

questions.questionTextEn: Let $A \in M_4(\mathbb{R})$ satisfy $A^2 + I_4 = 0$. Which of the following statements is ALWAYS true about $A$?
optionsEn: $A$ has only one similarity class over $\mathbb{C}$
questions.explanationEn: Since $m_A(t)$ divides $t^2 + 1$ and $A$ is real, the complex eigenvalues of $A$ are $+i$ and $-i$ occurring in conjugate pairs, so $+i$ and $-i$ each have algebraic multiplicity $2$. Therefore $\operatorname{tr}(A) = 2i + 2(-i) = 0$ and $\det(A) = i^2 (-i)^2 = (-1)(-1) = 1$. Note that $A$ need not be skew-symmetric (e.g., $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ -1 & -1 \end{pmatrix} \oplus \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ -1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$).

questions.questionTextEn: Let $D: P_4(\mathbb{R}) \to P_4(\mathbb{R})$ be the differentiation operator $D(p) = p'$. What is the minimal polynomial of $D$?
questions.explanationEn: On $P_4(\mathbb{R})$, $D^5(p) = 0$ for every polynomial of degree at most $4$, while $D^4(x^4) = 24 \neq 0$. Thus $D$ is nilpotent of index $5$, so its minimal polynomial is $t^5$.

questions.questionTextEn: Let $K \in M_n(\mathbb{R})$ be a real skew-symmetric matrix ($K^T = -K$). The Cayley transform $Q = (I - K)(I + K)^{-1}$ is ALWAYS:
questions.explanationEn: Since $K$ is skew-symmetric, $I + K$ is invertible and $K^T = -K$. Thus $Q^T Q = (I - K)^{-1}(I + K)(I - K)(I + K)^{-1} = I$ (as $I + K$ and $I - K$ commute), so $Q$ is orthogonal. Moreover, $\det(I - K) = \det((I - K)^T) = \det(I + K) \neq 0$, hence $\det(Q) = \frac{\det(I - K)}{\det(I + K)} = 1$.

questions.questionTextEn: Let $A \in M_{m \times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and $B \in M_{n \times p}(\mathbb{R})$. Which of the following is Sylvester's rank inequality?
questions.explanationEn: Restricting $A$ to $\operatorname{im}(B)$ gives $\operatorname{rank}(B) - \operatorname{rank}(AB) = \dim(\ker(A) \cap \operatorname{im}(B)) \le \dim(\ker(A)) = n - \operatorname{rank}(A)$. Rearranging yields Sylvester's rank inequality: $\operatorname{rank}(AB) \ge \operatorname{rank}(A) + \operatorname{rank}(B) - n$.

questions.questionTextEn: Let $A \in M_5(\mathbb{C})$ have characteristic polynomial $(t - 2)^5$ and minimal polynomial $(t - 2)^3$. Which of the following are POSSIBLE values for $\operatorname{rank}(A - 2I)$?
questions.explanationEn: Since $m_A(t) = (t - 2)^3$, the largest Jordan block has size $3$. The remaining size $5 - 3 = 2$ can be partitioned as $(2)$ or $(1, 1)$. Thus the possible Jordan block partitions are $(3, 2)$ (with $2$ blocks, so $\operatorname{nullity} = 2$ and $\operatorname{rank} = 5 - 2 = 3$) and $(3, 1, 1)$ (with $3$ blocks, so $\operatorname{nullity} = 3$ and $\operatorname{rank} = 5 - 3 = 2$). Hence possible ranks are $2$ and $3$.

questions.questionTextEn: Let $A \in M_n(\mathbb{C})$ be a normal matrix. Which of the following statements are ALWAYS true?
optionsEn: If all eigenvalues of $A$ are real, then $A$ is Hermitian
If all eigenvalues of $A$ have modulus $1$, then $A$ is unitary
questions.explanationEn: Write $A = U D U^*$ with $U$ unitary and $D = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n)$. If all $\lambda_i \in \mathbb{R}$, then $D^* = D \implies A^* = A$ (A). If all $|\lambda_i| = 1$, then $D^* D = I \implies A^* A = I$ (B). If $A$ is nilpotent, all $\lambda_i = 0 \implies D = 0 \implies A = 0$ (C). Finally $\|Av\| = \|A^* v\|$ for all $v$ implies $\ker(A) = \ker(A^*)$ (D).

questions.questionTextEn: Let $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$. Compute $\operatorname{tr}(A^5)$.
questions.explanationEn: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $2 + 1 = 3$ and $2 - 1 = 1$. Therefore the eigenvalues of $A^5$ are $3^5 = 243$ and $1^5 = 1$, giving $\operatorname{tr}(A^5) = 243 + 1 = 244$.

questions.questionTextEn: Let $A \in M_6(\mathbb{C})$ have Jordan blocks of sizes $3$ and $1$ for eigenvalue $0$, and a single Jordan block of size $2$ for eigenvalue $2$. What is $\operatorname{rank}(A^2)$?
questions.explanationEn: For the $3 \times 3$ nilpotent block $J_3(0)$, $\operatorname{rank}(J_3(0)^2) = 1$. For $J_1(0)$, $\operatorname{rank}(J_1(0)^2) = 0$. For the invertible $2 \times 2$ block $J_2(2)$, $\operatorname{rank}(J_2(2)^2) = 2$. Summing over blocks gives $\operatorname{rank}(A^2) = 1 + 0 + 2 = 3$.

questions.questionTextEn:
What is the rank of the real quadratic form
$$q(x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4) = x_1^2 + 2x_1 x_2 + 2x_2^2 + 2x_2 x_3 + 2x_3^2 + 2x_3 x_4 + x_4^2?$$
questions.explanationEn: Completing the square yields $q = (x_1 + x_2)^2 + (x_2 + x_3)^2 + (x_3 + x_4)^2$. The three linear forms $y_1 = x_1 + x_2$, $y_2 = x_2 + x_3$, and $y_3 = x_3 + x_4$ are linearly independent (with common kernel spanned by $(1, -1, 1, -1)^T$). Hence the rank of $q$ is $3$.
